summary.text: The ocean carbon cycle is the set of processes that move carbon between pools in the sea and between the sea, the air, the seafloor and Earth's interior.
Three pumps, called the solubility, carbonate and biological pumps, bring carbon dioxide from the air into the ocean interior and spread it through the oceans.
In recent decades the ocean has absorbed about a quarter of human CO₂ emissions, slowing the rise in the air but making seawater more acidic.

facts.label: Ocean's carbon share
facts.value: About 95% of active surface carbon (~38,000 Gt C)

facts.label: Marine life's yearly flux
facts.value: About 50 Gt C, like land plants

items.prompt: Ocean life holds only about 3 Gt of carbon, while land plants hold about 610 Gt. How do the amounts of carbon they exchange each year compare?

options.label: Land plants exchange about 200 times more
Ocean life exchanges almost none
They are nearly equal, about 50 Gt each
Ocean life exchanges ten times more

items.explain: Despite storing far less carbon, marine life exchanges nearly as much carbon each year as land vegetation, about 50 Gt C each.

items.prompt: Before the Industrial Revolution, which way did carbon dioxide flow overall between the ocean and the air?

options.label: The ocean gave off more than it took in
The ocean took in far more than today
No carbon dioxide moved either way
It only entered the sea through rivers

items.explain: Before the Industrial Revolution the ocean was a net source of CO₂ to the atmosphere; now most carbon entering it comes from the air.

items.prompt: The ocean has taken up a large share of the carbon dioxide people release. What is a downside of this?

options.label: Seawater gets much saltier
Seawater becomes more acidic
Sea levels start to fall
The ocean stops making oxygen

items.explain: Absorbing human-made CO₂ has slowed its rise in the air but has also acidified the oceans.

items.prompt: Seawater is pushed through a very fine filter. Bits of dead plankton and fecal matter get caught on it. What kind of carbon are they?

options.label: Dissolved organic carbon
Dissolved inorganic carbon
Particulate inorganic carbon
Particulate organic carbon

items.explain: Organic carbon caught on the filter is particulate organic carbon, which includes organisms, their fecal matter and detritus.

items.prompt: Deeper in the ocean there is more dissolved inorganic carbon and less free oxygen. What explains both?

options.label: Deep water is in closer contact with the air
High pressure turns oxygen into carbon
Sinking organic particles are respired, using oxygen
Deep water is warmer than surface water

items.explain: As organic particles sink and are respired, carbon is released as DIC and oxygen is used up.

items.prompt: What keeps the acidity of seawater from swinging wildly from day to day?

options.label: The steady cold of the deep sea
Bicarbonate and carbonate acting as a buffer
Dissolved oxygen neutralizing acids
Salt crystals soaking up the acid

items.explain: Bicarbonate and carbonate are major contributors to alkalinity, a natural buffer that prevents drastic changes in pH.
